ATLANTA, Georgia (CNN) -- The high-end specialty coffee industry isn't immune to the effects of a recession, but many companies are still doing well. Growers, roasters and equipment manufacturers were represented at the coffee expo in Atlanta. Portland Roasting had a slow holiday season, but business is picking up, said owner Mark Stell. "People don't leave coffee," he said. "They just get it differently." Tony Riffel owns Octane Coffee in Atlanta and was watching the 10th annual World Barista Championship, held in conjunction with the expo at the Georgia World Congress Center. Pushcart owner Gwilym Davies of London, England, won the 2009 barista crown.  Watch baristas battle for the world title » . Riffel said business at his coffee shop was flat last summer, but sales are up 10 percent for the first quarter of 2009. "The first part of this year has been our best ever," he said. "People are being careful with what they're spending money on, but they're spending it on quality products." Business is good enough that Riffel plans to open a second location this year. "Now is a really good time to do that," he said. "Developers and landlords are more flexible and negotiable," even though banks are "pickier than normal." Joseph Taguman also knows about picky banks. The general manager of the Zambia Growers Association said the lack of financing is holding back the association's 80 farmers. Taguman said the farmers could grow more than their current rate of about 300 metric tons per year, but trees take time to grow and long-term financing is hard to come by in Zambia. A couple of aisles over from Taguman's booth, Shawn Contreras sees a similar problem. Contreras is the sales director for Diedrich Manufacturing, which has been selling roasting equipment for nearly 30 years. He said wholesale roasters are continuing to grow, but smaller operations are having "an extraordinarily difficult time" getting funding. Consultant Andrew Hetzel acknowledges that credit is a hindering factor for companies, but he is optimistic about the specialty coffee industry. "The U.S. market is continuing at a steady pace," he said. But it's a slower pace than the past few years. "Coffee is something that has been with humanity for 1,500 years," Hetzel said. ATLANTA, Georgia (CNN) — Although the recession has affected the premium specialty-coffee sector, many businesses in the industry continue to perform strongly.

Coffee farmers, roasting companies and equipment makers gathered in Atlanta for the Specialty Coffee Association of America expo. Nearly 800 exhibits filled the event floor, displaying products ranging from rare beans to new Italian espresso machines.

Mark Stell, owner of Oregon-based Portland Roasting, traveled to Georgia for the show. He said his company experienced a weak holiday period, but sales have since improved, with February proving especially successful. Portland Roasting sells roughly 1 million pounds of coffee annually. While demand from hotels and offices has fallen, increased purchases by grocery stores and universities have made up the difference. According to Stell, consumers are not abandoning coffee; they are simply changing how they obtain it.

Atlanta’s Octane Coffee owner, Tony Riffel, attended the 10th World Barista Championship, which took place alongside the expo at the Georgia World Congress Center. Gwilym Davies, a London pushcart operator, captured the 2009 world barista title.

Riffel said his shop’s revenue was unchanged during the previous summer, but sales rose 10 percent in the first quarter of 2009. He described the opening months of the year as the strongest in the company’s history, explaining that customers were watching their spending while still choosing high-quality goods.

The business is doing well enough for Riffel to plan a second location before the end of the year. He believes current conditions make expansion attractive because property developers and landlords are more willing to negotiate, although banks have become more selective.

Financing is also a concern for Joseph Taguman, general manager of the Zambia Growers Association. He said difficulty securing funds is limiting the association’s 80 farmers. They currently produce approximately 300 metric tons of coffee each year and have the capacity to grow more, but coffee trees require time to mature, and long-term funding is difficult to obtain in Zambia.

A short distance from Taguman’s exhibit, Shawn Contreras reported a comparable challenge. Contreras, sales director for Diedrich Manufacturing, said the company has sold coffee-roasting machinery for almost three decades. Large wholesale roasters are still expanding, he noted, but small businesses are finding it exceptionally hard to obtain financing.

Industry consultant Andrew Hetzel agreed that restricted access to credit is impeding companies, yet he remained positive about specialty coffee’s prospects. He said the U.S. market continues to advance steadily, though more slowly than it did in recent years. In his view, coffee—part of human life for about 1,500 years—is unlikely to disappear anytime soon.

The specialty coffee industry is confronting the recession with cautious optimism. At a major trade expo in Atlanta, roasters, growers, equipment manufacturers, café owners, and other industry professionals gathered to showcase premium products, pursue new customers, and identify opportunities in a changing market.

The downturn has weakened some traditional sources of demand. Coffee suppliers that once relied heavily on corporate offices and hotels are seeing fewer orders as businesses reduce expenses and travel slows. At the same time, growers and smaller coffee companies are finding it more difficult to secure financing, limiting their ability to invest in crops, equipment, and expansion.

To compensate, many businesses are shifting their attention toward customers that have proved more resilient. Universities and similar institutions also offer relatively steady demand, giving suppliers an alternative to struggling hospitality and office accounts. Some companies are adapting their packaging, distribution, and product lines to serve these markets more effectively.

Despite the challenges, the mood across much of the industry remains positive. Many coffee businesses report that sales are still increasing, and some are moving ahead with plans to add locations, expand production, or enter new markets. Their experience suggests that specialty coffee has retained a loyal customer base even during difficult economic conditions.

Consumers may be changing where and how they buy coffee, but many still appear willing to pay more for quality, distinctive flavors, and responsibly sourced beans. Rather than abandoning specialty coffee, they may be purchasing it at supermarkets, brewing it at home, or seeking it out in settings other than offices and hotels. counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about how the specialty coffee industry is weathering the 2009 recession, using reporting from the Specialty Coffee Association of America expo in Atlanta.
counterfactuals.output:
# Specialty coffee finds a measure of comfort in recession

**ATLANTA, Georgia (CNN)** — On the crowded floor of the Specialty Coffee Association of America’s annual expo, the recession can be difficult to spot.

Baristas steam milk, buyers crowd around roasting machines and exhibitors offer samples of coffees from Ethiopia, Colombia and Central America. But beneath the caffeine-fueled bustle, nearly every conversation turns to the same question: How much will consumers continue to pay for a better cup of coffee?

So far, many in the specialty coffee business say the industry is holding up better than expected.

Coffee has long occupied a useful place in the consumer budget: It is a small indulgence, even when families are cutting back on restaurant meals, vacations and big-ticket purchases. A $3 latte may seem expensive compared with office coffee, but it is still cheaper than dinner out.

That has helped specialty coffee weather the downturn, according to roasters, café owners and equipment suppliers gathered in Atlanta. Yet the recession is changing where people drink coffee, what they order and how businesses compete for their dollars.

## An affordable luxury

Some café operators at the expo said customer traffic remains steady, but shoppers are becoming more cautious. They may skip a pastry, choose a smaller drink or make fewer visits each week. Others are trading down from elaborate espresso beverages to brewed coffee.

At the same time, more consumers appear interested in preparing better coffee at home. Exhibitors selling grinders, brewers and small roasting equipment reported strong interest from buyers who see home brewing as a way to save money without giving up quality.

That shift creates an opportunity for independent roasters and retailers selling whole beans. A bag of premium coffee may cost more than a supermarket brand, but it can produce many cups for the price of a few café drinks.

The message repeated across the trade-show floor was that specialty coffee must demonstrate value, not simply charge a premium.

That means fresher beans, careful preparation and employees who can explain why one coffee tastes different from another. In a recession, industry members said, customers are less willing to pay extra for a drink that is inconsistent or poorly made.

## Small operators feel the squeeze

The downturn is still taking a toll.

Independent coffee shops often operate on narrow margins and face rising costs for rent, health care, utilities and ingredients. Sales declines that a large chain might absorb can threaten the survival of a single neighborhood café.

Access to credit is another concern. Espresso machines and commercial roasters can cost tens of thousands of dollars, and banks have become more reluctant to lend. Equipment companies at the expo are emphasizing efficiency, durability and financing as café owners postpone major purchases.

Competition also remains intense. Specialty shops are no longer competing only with one another. Fast-food restaurants, convenience stores and mainstream chains have improved their coffee offerings, often at lower prices.

That has pushed independent cafés to focus on qualities that are harder to duplicate: personal service, local identity and close relationships with farmers and importers.

## Sustainability under pressure

The recession is also testing the industry’s commitment to environmental and social programs.

Over the past decade, specialty coffee companies have invested heavily in organic certification, fair-trade purchasing and direct relationships with growers. Those programs frequently add costs, raising questions about whether consumers will continue supporting them during a downturn.

Many exhibitors in Atlanta argued that sustainability is no longer an optional marketing feature. Long-term access to high-quality coffee depends on farmers earning enough to maintain their land and improve production, they said.

Still, café owners acknowledged that shoppers are paying closer attention to price. The challenge is explaining how higher prices can support better farming practices while also producing a better-tasting cup.

## Betting on quality

The expo’s competitions and demonstrations offered a counterpoint to the economic gloom. Baristas carefully weighed coffee, timed espresso shots and presented drinks to judges, while roasters compared flavor notes from individual farms and growing regions.

Such attention to detail may seem extravagant during the worst economic contraction in decades. But the industry is betting that quality will help it endure.

Specialty coffee has advantages that many luxury businesses do not. It is habitual, widely available and relatively inexpensive. For some consumers, the daily visit to a café also provides a sense of routine and community at a time of widespread anxiety.

No one in Atlanta was claiming immunity from the recession. Weak consumer spending, tight credit and aggressive price competition are forcing businesses to adapt.

But as samples continued to pour and buyers moved from booth to booth, the prevailing mood was cautious rather than bleak.

Consumers may delay buying a car or cancel a trip, industry members said. Many are not yet ready to give up their morning coffee.

# Economic Outlook for High-End Coffee Businesses During a Recession

*Scope: global specialty-coffee sector, with emphasis on mature consumer markets. Because no country or recession period was specified, this is a scenario-based outlook rather than a forecast for a particular economy.*

## Executive summary

High-end coffee is likely to prove more resilient than luxury restaurants or major discretionary purchases during a recession, but it is not recession-proof. Consumers often preserve small, affordable indulgences while cutting travel, dining, and merchandise spending. At the same time, some will reduce café visits, order simpler drinks, or brew more coffee at home.

The likely result is a **two-speed market**:

- Established cafés and roasters with loyal customers, strong brands, disciplined costs, and multiple sales channels can retain demand and possibly gain market share.
- Highly leveraged operators, marginal cafés, and businesses dependent on office traffic, expensive fit-outs, or occasional customers face greater risk.
- At-home specialty coffee, subscriptions, repair services, and lower-priced premium products should outperform new café construction and top-tier equipment sales.
- Growers remain the most exposed participants because recession-related demand pressure coincides with climate, financing, labor, and currency risks.

## Outlook by industry group

### 1. Coffee growers

**Perspective:** For specialty growers, the central concern is not simply whether consumers keep drinking coffee, but whether importers and roasters continue paying premiums for quality, traceability, and distinctive processing.

In a mild recession, demand for high-quality green coffee may remain relatively firm. Roasters generally cannot replace carefully sourced lots without affecting flavor and brand credibility. Long-term relationships can also protect established producers.

A deeper downturn would create several problems:

- Buyers may favor dependable, moderately priced coffees over rare microlots.
- Roasters may reduce forward commitments and hold less inventory.
- Importers could tighten credit or shorten payment terms.
- Consumers may resist price increases even as farm costs rise.
- Currency movements can help export revenue in some countries but make fertilizer, fuel, machinery, and debt more expensive.

Growers also face risks largely independent of the business cycle: climate volatility, water constraints, pests, rising wages, and uneven harvests. These factors can keep green-coffee prices elevated even while consumer demand weakens, squeezing margins elsewhere in the supply chain.

**Best positioned:** Diversified farms with reliable quality, direct buyer relationships, strong agronomy, manageable debt, and more than one export market.

**Most vulnerable:** Producers dependent on a few experimental lots, expensive processing methods, or buyers that treat premium coffee as an optional purchase.

### 2. Specialty roasters

**Perspective:** Roasters may benefit when customers replace café visits with home brewing, but wholesale accounts and premium product lines can weaken.

Expected changes include:

- More demand for blends and “approachable premium” coffees.
- Slower sales of rare single-origin lots and high-priced releases.
- Growth in subscriptions if they offer convenience and visible value.
- Pressure from cafés seeking lower wholesale prices or longer payment terms.
- Increased bad-debt risk if restaurant and café customers close.
- Margin pressure from packaging, freight, energy, wages, and green coffee.

Roasters with direct-to-consumer websites, grocery distribution, subscriptions, wholesale accounts, and their own cafés have several ways to offset weakness. However, excessive inventory can be dangerous because roasted coffee deteriorates and green coffee ties up working capital.

Premium roasters are therefore likely to emphasize smaller production runs, better demand forecasting, fewer overlapping products, and flexible sourcing. Some will introduce lower-priced blends rather than discount flagship coffees, protecting brand value while giving customers a trade-down option.

### 3. Café owners

**Perspective:** Cafés face the most immediate exposure to reduced foot traffic, rent, wages, utilities, and consumer price sensitivity.

Coffee remains a relatively affordable indulgence, which supports demand. Yet small changes in behavior—one fewer visit per week, switching from a milk drink to drip coffee, or declining food and merchandise—can materially reduce profit because café margins depend on volume and attachment sales.

Important variables include:

- **Location:** Neighborhood cafés may hold up better than sites tied to offices, tourism, or luxury retail.
- **Lease burden:** High fixed rent sharply reduces flexibility.
- **Labor model:** Businesses need enough staff for service quality but cannot carry excess scheduling.
- **Menu engineering:** Simple menus, batch brew, bakery items, and efficient food programs can protect margins.
- **Customer loyalty:** Memberships, prepaid accounts, and subscriptions can stabilize cash flow.
- **Speed and convenience:** Mobile ordering and takeaway service can matter more as customers scrutinize both time and money.

Cafés should be cautious about broad discounting. Frequent promotions can train customers to wait for deals without fixing the underlying cost structure. Better options include smaller sizes, entry-priced drinks, bundles, loyalty rewards, and premium add-ons for customers still willing to spend.

Independent operators with weak balance sheets are vulnerable even when sales decline only modestly. Rent negotiations, cash reserves, inventory control, and daily labor management may be more decisive than headline revenue.

### 4. Equipment manufacturers and distributors

**Perspective:** The equipment sector is usually more cyclical because espresso machines, grinders, brewers, and roasting systems are capital purchases that can be postponed.

Likely recession effects include:

- Delayed café openings and renovations.
- Longer replacement cycles for commercial machines.
- Greater demand for leasing, financing, and refurbished equipment.
- Stronger sales of parts, maintenance contracts, and repair services.
- Interest in equipment that reduces labor, energy, waste, or training requirements.
- Mixed home-equipment demand: entry and midrange products may benefit from home brewing, while luxury machines remain dependent on affluent buyers.

Manufacturers with recurring service revenue and robust dealer networks should be more resilient than firms reliant on new installations. Customers will increasingly demand a clear payback calculation—for example, lower energy use, automated milk systems, reduced coffee waste, or fewer staff hours.

Credit conditions are critical. Even operators confident about demand may cancel purchases if financing becomes expensive or unavailable.

### 5. Industry consultants

**Perspective:** Consultants generally view specialty coffee as resilient but increasingly polarized. Affluent consumers may continue buying exceptional coffee, while middle-income customers seek value. The difficult position is an undifferentiated premium offer: expensive enough to invite scrutiny but not distinctive enough to inspire loyalty.

Consultants are likely to advise businesses to focus on:

1. **Cash flow over expansion.** Preserve liquidity and stress-test revenue declines.
2. **Clear positioning.** Compete through exceptional quality, convenience, community, or value—not vague “premium” branding.
3. **Channel diversification.** Combine cafés, wholesale, e-commerce, subscriptions, and selected retail distribution.
4. **Customer retention.** Existing customers are cheaper to keep than new ones are to acquire.
5. **Simplified operations.** Reduce low-volume menu items and unnecessary stock-keeping units.
6. **Supplier relationships.** Renegotiate terms without shifting unsustainable risk onto growers.
7. **Selective investment.** Fund projects with short, measurable payback periods.

Consulting demand itself may be mixed. Strategy, turnaround, menu profitability, lease negotiation, and operational-efficiency work can increase, while brand redesigns and ambitious expansion projects may be postponed.

## Expected performance by segment

| Segment | Recession outlook | Main risk | Relative opportunity |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rare microlots and auction coffees | Soft to volatile | Customers trade down | Small affluent niche remains |
| Premium blends | Relatively resilient | Margin compression | Strong value-to-quality proposition |
| Café beverages | Moderate decline in frequency or ticket size | High fixed costs | Affordable-indulgence effect |
| At-home beans and subscriptions | Stable to positive | Subscriber churn | Shift from cafés to home brewing |
| Wholesale roasting | Mixed | Café and restaurant closures | Winning accounts from weaker competitors |
| New commercial equipment | Weak | Deferred capital spending | Automation with rapid payback |
| Repairs and refurbished equipment | Positive | Parts and technician shortages | Customers extend asset life |
| Luxury home machines | Polarized | Discretionary-spending cuts | Affluent enthusiasts remain active |

## Recession scenarios

### Mild recession

The sector experiences slower growth rather than broad contraction. Consumers visit cafés slightly less often but continue buying quality coffee. Home brewing and subscriptions grow. Café closures are concentrated among already weak operators, and established brands acquire sites or customers at lower cost.

### Severe or prolonged recession

Trade-down behavior becomes pronounced. Café visits, food attachments, and equipment purchases fall. Wholesale defaults increase, financing tightens, and consolidation accelerates. Growers struggle to secure premiums for unusual coffees even if production costs remain high.

### Stagflationary downturn

This is the most difficult scenario. Consumer demand weakens while coffee, milk, energy, rent, packaging, and wages remain expensive. Businesses cannot fully pass costs through and margins compress across the chain. Operational efficiency and balance-sheet strength become especially important.

## Indicators to monitor

Businesses should track more than overall coffee consumption:

- Café transactions versus average ticket size
- Customer visit frequency and loyalty-program activity
- Sales mix between espresso drinks, batch brew, food, and retail beans
- Subscription acquisition, retention, and cancellation rates
- Green-coffee prices and quality differentials
- Freight, packaging, dairy, energy, and labor costs
- Wholesale customer payment delays
- Commercial vacancy rates and landlord concessions
- Equipment-financing rates and approval standards
- Consumer confidence among middle- and high-income households

## Bottom line

The high-end coffee industry should retain a meaningful base of demand during a recession because coffee is habitual, culturally embedded, and inexpensive relative to larger luxuries. Nevertheless, resilience at the category level does not guarantee profitability for individual firms.

The strongest businesses will be those that offer recognizable quality at a defensible price, maintain close customer and supplier relationships, control fixed costs, and serve both café and at-home consumption. The weakest will be heavily indebted, operationally complex, dependent on continual expansion, or positioned as premium without demonstrating clear value.

## CNN Business Feature Package  
**Location:** Georgia World Congress Center, Atlanta  
**Working title:** **“Specialty Coffee’s High-Stakes Growth Bet”**  
**Estimated runtime:** 3:30–4:00  
**Format:** Anchor intro, reporter package, live tag  
**Editorial note:** Confirm event name, attendance, company figures, prices, and all quotations before broadcast.

---

### ANCHOR INTRO

For millions of Americans, coffee is a daily ritual. But behind each specialty cup is an industry contending with higher costs, cautious lenders and changing consumer habits.

At the Georgia World Congress Center in Atlanta, coffee entrepreneurs are showcasing new products while weighing how—and whether—to expand.

CNN’s **[REPORTER NAME]** looks at the financial pressures facing the industry and why many business owners remain optimistic.

---

## REPORTER PACKAGE

### 00:00–00:15 — OPEN

**VIDEO:** Wide shots of the convention floor; espresso pouring; milk steaming; exhibitors speaking with buyers; close-up of latte art.

**NAT SOUND:** Grinder, steam wand, crowd noise.

**REPORTER TRACK:**  
Inside the Georgia World Congress Center, specialty coffee is part craft, part culture—and increasingly, a high-stakes business.

Every cup on display represents a long supply chain: farmers, exporters, roasters, equipment makers and café owners, all navigating rising expenses and an uncertain economy.

---

### 00:15–00:50 — SALES AND CONSUMER DEMAND

**VIDEO:** Baristas serving samples; customers examining packaged beans; point-of-sale transaction; retail displays.

**REPORTER TRACK:**  
Specialty coffee companies are betting consumers will continue paying more for quality, convenience and a story about where their coffee comes from.

Sales opportunities now extend beyond the neighborhood café. Roasters are pursuing grocery shelves, online subscriptions, offices, hotels and ready-to-drink products.

But growth is not guaranteed. Customers may still want premium coffee while cutting back on how often they buy it away from home.

**SOUNDBITE — ROASTER OR CAFÉ OWNER:**  
*Suggested topic: Current sales, customer traffic, pricing and whether shoppers are trading down.*

**LOWER THIRD:**  
**[NAME]**  
**[TITLE], [COMPANY]**

**REPORTER TRACK:**  
That forces businesses to balance affordability with margins already squeezed by labor, rent, packaging, shipping and volatile green-coffee costs.

---

### 00:50–01:40 — FINANCING CHALLENGES

**VIDEO:** Commercial espresso machines; roasting equipment; entrepreneur reviewing a loan proposal; booth featuring payment or lending services.

**REPORTER TRACK:**  
Opening a café or expanding a roasting operation requires significant upfront investment. Commercial machines can cost tens of thousands of dollars, before construction, permits, inventory or payroll.

For smaller operators, obtaining that money can be difficult. Traditional lenders often want collateral, a strong operating history and predictable cash flow—conditions a young hospitality business may struggle to meet.

Higher borrowing costs can also change the math.

Technology may create additional efficiencies, from automated brewing and inventory management to loyalty programs that help businesses understand—and retain—their customers.

## LIVE TAG / ANCHOR Q&A

**ANCHOR:**  
What are business owners telling you is their biggest concern?

**REPORTER:**  
The most consistent concern is the combined cost of growth. Equipment, construction, labor and inventory are all expensive, and financing can be harder to secure or more costly than owners expected. Even companies with strong sales are being more selective about new locations and are looking at lower-capital options such as wholesale, subscriptions and smaller-format cafés.

**ANCHOR:**  
Where is the optimism coming from?

**REPORTER:**  
Coffee remains a frequent, often habitual purchase, and specialty businesses believe consumers still value quality and experience. The optimism is strongest among companies that have multiple ways to reach customers rather than relying only on café traffic.

## KEY QUESTIONS

### For café owners and roasters
- How have sales changed over the past year?  
- Have customers resisted price increases?  
- What does it cost to open or expand a location?  
- Have you delayed growth because of financing conditions?  
- Which channel offers the best margins: cafés, wholesale, online or ready-to-drink?  
- What gives you confidence about the next 12 months?

### For lenders
- What makes a coffee business financeable?  
- What are the most common reasons applications are rejected?  
- How much equity or collateral is typically expected?  
- Are equipment leases or government-backed loans becoming more important?  

### For analysts
- Is specialty coffee outperforming the wider restaurant sector?  
- Are consumers trading down or simply buying coffee less frequently?  
- Which expansion models carry the least risk?  
- How could climate and commodity-price volatility affect retail prices?
